> the number of operations needed to solve satisfiability will always be exponential in the size of the problem, no matter what algorithm is chosen

A common complexity theory misunderstanding is that statements like this applies to all or even most instances-- and it leads to objectively bad engineering of the form "oh look this is actually 3sat, it's unsolvable".

(Great fodder for a midwit meme: idiot and genius say "my heuristics go brrr!"-- midwit says "No no no! NP problems can't be efficiently solved!")

  In computer science, the satisfiability problem is the task of determining whether a boolean problem can be satisfied, that is, made to be true, by some combination of inputs. For example, the expression: A AND NOT B is satisfied whenever A is true and B is false, while the expression: A AND NOT A cannot be satisfied.
  A naive approach to satisfiablilty would be to check every possible input and see if the expression evaluates to true. 
  However, the number of combinations that must be checked is 2n, where n is the number of variables in the expression. This is what is meant by exponential time.
  The exponential time hypothesis conjectures that you cannot do better, that is, the number of operations needed to solve satisfiability will always be exponential in the size of the problem, no matter what algorithm is chosen.
  If this hypothesis is true, it would imply that P≠NP, because satisfiability has been shown to be in NP, and in order for it to be in P there would have to exist an algorithm that solves it in polynomial time.

The exponential time hypothesis is essentially that NP-complete problems' best solutions are all exponential.

NP-complete problems are essentially those where you need to make some kind of choice over a superlinearly-growing set of options where each option can be solved in polynomial time. Like, for example, finding a route between cities on a map under a certain total distance. You might need to go over all choices of routes.

The ETH essentially assumes that the best solution (in terms of complexity, i.e. how it grows) you can get for these kinds of problems is exponential. children.author: SyzygyRhythm
children.text:
There's a set of problems that are (it is conjectured) easy to verify but hard to solve. One of them, called 3SAT, looks for values (a, b, c, ...) such that an expression like ((a or b or c) and (b or not-c or e) and ...) evaluates to true. And it turns out that all of these supposedly hard problems can be converted to 3SAT, so if you find a solution to one you find a solution to all.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis in effect says that 3SAT can only be solved by brute force--trying every possible combination until you find the right one. If your 3SAT expression has 100 variables, then this will take about 2^100 tries (exponential time).

What they found was an algorithm faster than brute force. 3SAT is still potentially one of these hard problems, but finding anything faster than brute force is a major advance.

the language around complexity domains is really confusing.

P means "this problem can be solved in polynomial # of steps relative to the problem size"

NP means "we don't know if the problem can be solved in polynomial # of steps relative to problem size, but we know we can check if the result is correct in a polynomial # of steps relative to the problem size"

!ETH: it was widely suspected that the flagship problem in NP, 3SAT, requires an exponential # of steps relative to problem size. We now know that 3SAT requires AT MOST something more than polynomial but strictly less than exponential to solve.

"P = NP" means "if you can check it in polynomial time, there's some way to solve it in polynomial time". "P != NP" means "there are some problems checkable in polynomial time for which there is no polynomial way to obtain the result"

Today's new proof makes "P = NP" "feel more likely", because we know that the flagship problem in NP is not exponential.

> To explain more, it is guaranteed that you can reduce any NP problem to 3SAT in polynomial time with a polynomial factor in input size.

No, subexponential is not the same as polynomial time. There's sub-exponential functions that grow faster than polynomial.

This is an amazing and unexpected result. To be clear though, it does not imply that NP is subexponential: "Note that runtime bounds of the form 2^o(n) do not transfer under general polynomial-time reductions (2^n^o(1) would be needed for this), so our result does not imply that general NP problems admit subexponential time algorithms."

Edit: To explain more, it is guaranteed that you can reduce any NP problem to 3SAT in polynomial time with a polynomial factor in input size. You still have to solve it.

If 3SAT were solvable in polynomial time, then polynomial(polynomial(x)) = polynomial(x) and you're implied to have an overall polynomial time solution.

But what we have here is that 3SAT is solveable in subexponential time. subexponential(polynomial(x)) is not guaranteed to be sub-exponential.

Further edit: The subexponential solution does carry over to any (?) problems that have can be reduced to 3SAT in a linear number of variables. They list: Counting independent sets, Counting proper q-colorings, Counting perfect matchings.

And that's fine. But here the question is perfectly well specified and properly formulated and not ambiguous at all.

The problem is that this formal question might not correspond to the informal question we actually care about.
It is completely acceptable in math to use "ill-posed" to indicate that something is insufficiently specified, improperly formulated, or ambiguous. Math people do this all the time.

> "Ill-posed" here means that the formalisms we've chosen to represent "efficient" and "efficiently verifiable" algorithms could turn out to not correspond to anything humans would consider meaningful ("we posed the problem poorly").

OK, that's a reasonable worry and one that practitioners share. Thanks for explaining. Though I don't think ill-posed is a good term for this, the technical meaning of the term points in a different direction.

So far, as far as I can tell this new result gives much of any extra credence to that worry.

"Ill-posed" here means that the formalisms we've chosen to represent "efficient" and "efficiently verifiable" algorithms could turn out to not correspond to anything humans would consider meaningful ("we posed the problem poorly"). For most people, a solution to an NP-complete problem that's barely-subexponential would be clear evidence of these formalisms being ill-posed.

There are many ways it might turn out to be ill-posed, this is just one of them. Impagliazzo's "5 worlds" survey is in some sense a catalog of some of these ways, and includes some of the ways you seem to be referencing (approxmations, probabilistic techniques, average-case efficiency; depending what you mean this could lie in the "Heuristica" world).

> Perhaps this will be the push we need to finally, seriously consider the possibility that our formalisms of “efficient” and “efficiently verifiable” algorithms correspond to nothing resembling reality,

What do you mean? Do you mean that our heuristics shortcuts of treating P as efficiently solvable (and NP as efficiently verifiable) are not warranted? So far pretty much all algorithms in P that we found have small exponents. That hasn't changed, but it might change in the future.

Or do you mean something else?

Keep in mind that even most instances of many NP hard problems can be solved very efficiently in practice, because most instances ain't hard.

However we know problems that are expected to be 'easier' than NP that are hard to solve in practice. These are pretty much all the problems we build cryptography out of, because essentially these problems are in the intersection of NP and co-NP and that's expected to be smaller than NP. And cryptography has to be hard to break on average to work: a random key needs to be a good key.

> and P \in NP is actually ill-posed.

Oh, that's very simple to answer: P is not an element of NP. The question people care about is whether there's any element in NP that's not in P. In LaTeX notation P \subset NP vs P \subseteq NP.

I'm not sure what you mean by ill-posed? The question is very clear. What are you trying to say?

Perhaps this will be the push we need to finally, seriously consider the possibility that our formalisms of “efficient” and “efficiently verifiable” algorithms correspond to nothing resembling reality, and P \in NP is actually ill-posed.

This has been marginally debated since the mid 90s, when Impagliazzo published the “5 worlds” survey. Occasionally it is brought up in talks about average case analysis. There is occasionally a workshop about it. But it has never really got the attention it deserved. How many more of these results do we need to take it seriously? (Assuming we do indeed certify it.)

for context (ai convo):

You're right, and I should correct my earlier phrasing. The paper does *not* merely assert existence — it gives a *specific deterministic algorithm* with a concrete, proven running time:

> A deterministic algorithm that exactly counts the satisfying assignments of a canonically encoded $k$-CNF formula on $n$ variables in time $(n+m)^{O_k(1)} \cdot 2^{O_k(n \log\log n / \sqrt{\log n})}$, using polynomial space.

The Lean formalization proves this bound. So it's a fully specified algorithm, not just "there exists one." My earlier "theoretical existence statement" framing was wrong.

*What that changes (and doesn't) for the practicality question:*

- It's a real algorithm in the sense that if you implemented it, it would terminate and give the correct answer. The proof guarantees the bound. - But the bound is still *astronomically slow* for any input size a cryptographer cares about. At $n = 1{,}000$ variables the exponent is already $\sim 1{,}000 \cdot 5 / 5 \approx 1{,}000$, i.e. $2^{1000}$ — far beyond any feasible computation. - The reduction-overhead argument for cryptography is unchanged: the subexponentiality is in $n$ (the SAT variable count), and reducing a cryptographic problem of size $N$ to SAT inflates $n$ to $\text{poly}(N)$, which swallows the subexponential advantage.

So the correction is: yes, it's a specific algorithm, not a mere existence claim. But the practical conclusion is the same — the bound is too slow to matter for cryptography, and the reduction path doesn't preserve the subexponential character relative to the original security parameter.

Linear programming admits a worst-case polynomial time algorithm.

It is notable that simplex, especially dual simplex is often better in practice, especially for integer linear programming with branch and bound because you only have to slightly modify the parent optimal basis in simplex vs entirely restarting or refactorizing for interior point methods.

There are hard problems where the worst case may be exponentially hard, but the average case is much faster. Linear programming and the traveling salesman problem are like that. The faster approaches are considered "probabilistic solutions".

In cryptography, most of the problems believed to be exponentially hard, such as factoring, don't have proofs of an exponential lower bound. There's some risk of a breakthrough that makes those problems easier. A probabilistic solution would be good enough to break many cryptosystems.

See his answer to the seventeenth question in this interview:

https://www.informit.com/articles/article.aspx?p=2213858&WT....

> Don Knuth: As you say, I've come to believe that P = N P, namely that there does exist an integer M and an algorithm that will solve every n-bit problem belonging to the class N P in n**M elementary steps.

I believe this stems from an incomplete understanding of the problem space on my part (excuse the multiple puns); but, I am skeptical Knuth really said P=NP. There are so many mathemtical examples of equations that clearly show P≠NP. Computing in itself was originally formed from using iterative methods to solve hard problems. Least-squares methods, sin() cos(), traveling salesman, so many to list? To say P=NP for all problems seems  like a fools errand to me.

While this has no immediate bearing on P-vs-NP, it is interesting to note:

- Early CS researchers like Donald Knuth entered CS in the days when regularly someone would come up with a surprising faster algorithm for some problem, and their intuitions were that most problems had faster algorithms than you'd expect.

- Later generations of CS researchers, as all the easy algorithms were discovered, and post Karp's definition of NP-completeness (and the Garey & Johnson book, say), began to specialize in proving hardness, and complexity theory with a “zoo” of complexity classes became more about separation and lower bounds, e.g. I've seen algorithms like Arora's PTAS for Euclidean TSP being described as a “failed attempt to prove a lower bound”. So an entire generation of researchers' intuition was mostly in the direction of an elegant universe with neat separation results (even if we couldn't get them).

- So e.g. surveys of computer scientists showed most of them believing that P≠NP, and someone like Knuth has always seemed a bit of an outlier for saying that maybe P=NP: his argument was simply that there are so many possible polynomial-time algorithms that we haven't explored, and maybe one of them with a large exponent could solve NP-complete problems. (In response to arguments that many researchers have failed to find any such algorithms, he would say that many researchers have failed to prove that P≠NP.) E.g. in 2017 when Scott Aaronson wrote his survey (https://www.scottaaronson.com/papers/pnp.pdf = https://www.scottaaronson.com/papers/pnp-kindle.pdf) he wrote:

> Admittedly, it can be hard to tell whether declarations that P = NP are meant seriously, or are merely attempts to be contrarian. However, we can surely agree with Knuth and Lipton that we’re far from understanding the limits of efficient computation, and that there are further surprises in store.
